question: The real elbow is soft: it sags and rests short of its target. Is that a setting inside the servos, and what are the gain settings on the real arm?
measure: The P, I and D coefficient registers of all six servos, read from the real arm without writing anything. P is the proportional gain: how hard the servo pushes per unit of position error. A lower P gives a softer joint. The factory value is 32.
outcome: Every servo reads P 16, D 32, I 0. That is half the factory P, and it is exactly what the LeRobot driver writes when it connects. Before the read, the SO-101 became the base simulator model with its own measured-servo scene (teacher 30 of 30).
setup: The arm has six servos (the motors in the joints): shoulder pan, shoulder lift, elbow flex, wrist flex, wrist roll and gripper. Each is a P servo: it pushes toward its target with a force proportional to how far away it is, scaled by a gain called P. With a low P and gravity pulling on the arm, a joint settles a little short of its target. In October a probe measured this softness on the real arm, and a servo model was fitted so the simulator could copy it (experiment 39). The handoff note of 2026-11-05 pointed at a likely cause: LeRobot, the robot driver library, writes P 16 (factory 32) when it connects, and the value likely persists in the servo. Experiment 42 showed that a policy trained around the soft servo fails on a stiff one. So it matters which end the real arm sits on. The teacher is the scripted program that solves the task in the simulator; its certification is 30 rollouts. A scene is one version of the simulator. This experiment has two halves: make the SO-101 arm model (experiment 43) the base with a soft-servo scene of its own, then read the real registers.

parts.title: Refit the October servo measurements through the SO-101 model
parts.why: The measured-servo scene existed only for the SO-100. The physics randomization recipe needs one for the SO-101.
parts.did: Ran the servo-model fit again on the October probe recordings, this time through the SO-101 scene. The error is the rms gap between the simulated and the recorded joint, in joint units, on the fit recordings.
parts.conclusion: The elbow is the joint the stiff model gets wrong (3.397 units), and a fitted stiffness of 6.481 instead of 50 brings it to 0.798. The other joints change little.

parts.title: Does the teacher certify on the SO-101 servo scene?
parts.why: A scene is only usable for capture if the teacher solves it. On a soft servo the teacher has to compensate for the sag.
parts.did: Built the scene bench_pick_replace_v1_so101_servo and certified the compensated teacher with two settings of its direction-slew compensation.
parts.conclusion: The scene uses 0.2. The runner also gained an ACT path that refuses to run a policy on a scene other than the one it was trained on.

parts.title: What do the real servos say?
parts.why: If P is 16 the softness is a setting, the real arm sits toward the soft end, and writing 32 back is an option.
parts.did: Plugged the arm in and ran tools/read_servo_registers.py, a read-only tool whose test asserts it never writes. The record is stamped 2026-11-13 00:38 UTC; the project notes date the read Nov 12.
parts.conclusion: All six servos hold the LeRobot values, not the factory ones. The tool's verdict: "lerobot_configure (P 16, written by robot.connect())". The settings were locked, torque was off, and the supply read 5.4 V (5.3 V on the gripper). Nothing was written back; restoring P 32 is the owner's call.

trust.text: The reader is read-only and its test asserts it never writes
Two later reads on Nov 15 give the same P 16 on every servo
The fit uses real recordings: four October probe runs and live episode 10
The servo model comes from one probe session in October
P 16 explains softness in general. Nobody has measured how much of the elbow's sag it accounts for (the handoff says "part of").
The registers were read with torque off, at rest

meaning: The softness is a driver setting shared by all six joints, not a hardware fault, and the real arm sits at the soft setting. That supports using the soft-servo scenes as the real-arm stand-in, and it kept the plan of experiment 45: train across soft to stiff so the policy does not depend on which value is in the registers. It also leaves a cheap lever unused: writing P 32 back would make the real arm stiffer.
lesson: Before modelling a hardware quirk, read the hardware's own settings. A two-minute read-only check explained a behaviour that had been measured and modelled for a month.

next.why: Done as experiment 45, built on this scene.

next.title: Decide whether to write P 32 back
next.why: Not done. It would change the real arm's response, so every servo scene would need refitting.
